subtopic_detail: separating recurrent wheeze occurring only with colds from asthma needing a daily preventer
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 2 year old boy brought by his father after a fourth episode of wheeze in twelve months. Each episode has begun with a runny nose and a cough, lasted about five days, and settled completely.

His father says that between episodes he runs around the park without stopping, sleeps through the night, and has never coughed at night or after running when he is well. He has no eczema and no food allergies, and neither parent nor either sibling has asthma, hay fever or eczema. He attends childcare three days a week. He was born at term and has never been admitted to hospital. Today he is at the end of an episode, is not distressed, and his chest is clear on auscultation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Speaking in phrases and playing, no accessory muscle use or tracheal tug, chest clear with no wheeze audible today, no eczema, growth tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start a daily inhaled corticosteroid preventer and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: A daily preventer is indicated where there are interval symptoms between illnesses, frequent severe episodes or a strong atopic background, none of which he has. Trials in this pattern of wheeze show daily inhaled corticosteroid does not reduce episode frequency or severity, so it commits a toddler to continuous treatment without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Start a daily oral leukotriene receptor antagonist taken through the winter months
options.rationale: Montelukast has been trialled both continuously and intermittently in this age group with modest and inconsistent benefit, and it carries a recognised risk of neuropsychiatric adverse effects including sleep disturbance and behavioural change in young children. It is not a first line answer for a child with no interval symptoms. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to aeroallergens before deciding on any preventer
options.rationale: Allergy testing contributes to the assessment of a child with interval symptoms or eczema where an atopic phenotype would change the threshold for preventer treatment. In a child with no personal or family atopy and no symptoms between illnesses it will not alter the plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Provide an inhaled bronchodilator with a spacer and a written action plan
options.rationale: Wheeze confined to viral illnesses with complete freedom between them and no atopic background is the pattern that resolves in most children by school age, so treatment is directed at episodes rather than at maintenance. Salbutamol through a spacer with a written plan setting out dosing and when to seek help gives the family control of the episodes without exposing him to continuous therapy that has not been shown to help this phenotype. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

options.text: Prescribe a course of oral prednisolone for the family to begin at each illness
options.rationale: Parent initiated oral corticosteroid has been studied in this pattern of wheeze and does not reduce hospital admission or symptom duration, while repeated courses in a preschooler carry growth and bone effects. Oral corticosteroid is reserved for an episode severe enough to require medical assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma)

explanation.summary: Preschool wheeze divides into a viral triggered pattern and a multiple trigger pattern, and the distinction determines whether maintenance treatment is worthwhile. This boy wheezes only with viral illnesses, is entirely well between them, and has no personal or family atopy, which places him firmly in the viral triggered group that usually resolves by school age. Randomised evidence shows that daily inhaled corticosteroid does not reduce the frequency or severity of episodes in this phenotype. Management is therefore episodic, with a bronchodilator delivered by spacer and a written action plan so the family knows what to give and when to seek review. Interval symptoms, atopy or escalating severity would change that assessment and prompt a preventer trial.
key_points: Complete freedom from symptoms between illnesses characterises viral triggered wheeze.
Daily inhaled corticosteroid does not reduce episode frequency or severity in this phenotype.
A personal or family history of atopy raises the likelihood of asthma and lowers the threshold for a preventer.
A spacer is as effective as a nebuliser for delivering bronchodilator in preschool children.
Parent initiated oral corticosteroid has not been shown to shorten episodes or prevent admission.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the child coughs at night or after running when completely well, because interval symptoms are what separate asthma from viral triggered wheeze and determine whether a daily preventer will do anything at all in a child under three.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

subtopic_detail: recognising heavy proteinuria in a preschooler whose facial swelling has been treated as an allergy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old girl referred by her general practitioner. Her mother first noticed puffiness around both eyes three weeks ago, worst on waking and easing through the day, and a locum prescribed an antihistamine for presumed allergy.

The swelling has not improved and over the past week her abdomen has become distended and her ankles swollen, so that her shoes no longer fit. She has had no rash, no urticaria and no wheeze, and there has been no new pet, detergent or food. She has passed normal coloured urine throughout and has had no dysuria and no fever. She had a sore throat about six weeks ago that settled without treatment. Her blood pressure is normal for her age and her growth is on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked periorbital oedema, pitting oedema to both mid shins, abdominal distension with shifting dullness, no rash or purpura, no joint swelling, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick protein 4 plus with no blood, urine protein creatinine ratio markedly raised, serum albumin 16 g/L (35-50), total cholesterol 9.1 mmol/L (less than 5.5), creatinine 32 micromol/L (20-50), complement C3 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Continue the antihistamine and add a short course of topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: Antihistamine treatment addresses histamine mediated angioedema, which appears over minutes to hours, is often asymmetrical and is usually accompanied by urticaria or a trigger. Three weeks of progressive symmetrical oedema with 4 plus proteinuria and an albumin of 16 g/L is a renal problem rather than an allergic one. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent percutaneous renal biopsy before commencing any drug treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for features that make minimal change disease unlikely, such as age under one or over twelve years, macroscopic haematuria, hypertension, impaired renal function or low complement, and for children who fail to respond to corticosteroid. None of those applies here, so biopsy would add an invasive procedure to a presentation with a predictable histology. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Give intravenous albumin with furosemide and observe the diuretic response
options.rationale: Albumin with a diuretic is used for severe symptomatic oedema causing respiratory compromise, scrotal or vulval oedema, or skin breakdown, and it carries a risk of pulmonary oedema and rebound fluid shift. She is comfortable with normal oxygen saturation, so it treats a complication she does not yet have rather than the disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Start oral penicillin and await antistreptolysin O titres before further treatment
options.rationale: A preceding sore throat raises post streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is the intended distractor, and that condition produces a nephritic picture with haematuria, hypertension, oedema and a low complement C3. Her urine contains no blood, her blood pressure is normal and her C3 is normal, which excludes it. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone daily with a planned taper after four weeks
options.rationale: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hypercholesterolaemia in a child between one and twelve years with normal blood pressure, no haematuria and normal renal function is minimal change disease in the great majority of cases, and around nine in ten such children enter remission on corticosteroid alone. Treatment is therefore started empirically without histology, with daily dosing for four weeks followed by an alternate day taper, alongside pneumococcal protection and counselling about the risk of peritonitis and thrombosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

explanation.summary: Periorbital oedema that is worst on waking is regularly misattributed to allergy, and the distinguishing features are that it is symmetrical, progressive over weeks, unaccompanied by urticaria or a trigger, and associated with dependent oedema later in the day. The diagnostic combination is heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hypercholesterolaemia. In a child aged one to twelve with normal blood pressure, no haematuria, normal renal function and normal complement, minimal change disease accounts for the great majority of cases and responds to corticosteroid, so treatment is empirical and biopsy is not required. The preceding sore throat is a deliberate lead towards post streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is excluded by the absent haematuria, normal blood pressure and normal complement C3. Children need counselling about infection and thrombosis, since urinary loss of immunoglobulin and antithrombin drives both.
key_points: Proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hypercholesterolaemia together define the nephrotic syndrome.
Minimal change disease predominates between one and twelve years and responds to corticosteroid in about nine in ten children.
Biopsy is indicated for atypical age, haematuria, hypertension, renal impairment, low complement or steroid resistance.
A nephritic picture with haematuria, hypertension and a low complement C3 suggests post streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Urinary loss of immunoglobulin and antithrombin causes susceptibility to pneumococcal peritonitis and to thrombosis.
explanation.pearls: Dipstick the urine of every child presenting with periorbital swelling before accepting an allergic explanation, because nephrotic syndrome is regularly treated with antihistamines for weeks, and swelling that is worst on waking with no urticaria and no trigger is renal until the dipstick says otherwise.

subtopic_detail: choosing between oral and intravenous glucose for a large newborn of a diabetic mother whose repeat sugar stays low
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward at two hours of age. The baby is a term boy born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery weighing 4 420 g to a mother whose pregnancy was complicated by insulin treated gestational diabetes.

He was put to the breast at thirty minutes and fed briefly. A routine pre feed blood glucose at one hour was 1.9 mmol/L, so the midwife gave 0.5 mL/kg of 40 percent oral glucose gel and a breastfeed, and the repeat pre feed level one hour later is 1.6 mmol/L. He is pink and well perfused, has a normal cry, has not had a seizure and is not jittery at present. His temperature has been stable since birth and there are no respiratory signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142/min, blood pressure 64/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well perfused with a capillary refill of 2 seconds, normal tone and normal cry, anterior fontanelle soft, no respiratory distress, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Pre feed blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L at one hour, repeat pre feed blood glucose 1.6 mmol/L at two hours, formal laboratory glucose sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: A second dose of 40 percent oral glucose gel with a further breastfeed
options.rationale: Buccal glucose gel with a feed is the correct first response and may be repeated, but it has now been given once and the level has fallen rather than risen, which is the point at which repeating it becomes a delay rather than a treatment. Most protocols permit at most two gel doses and none accept a falling level as a reason to repeat. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Top up with expressed breast milk hourly and recheck in three hours
options.rationale: Increasing enteral intake is the mainstay while levels are responding, and a three hour gap is far too long once a level below 2.0 mmol/L has failed to correct. Neuroglycopenic injury in the newborn is not signalled reliably by symptoms, so the interval between checks must shorten rather than lengthen. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give an intramuscular glucagon dose and continue to feed on the ward
options.rationale: Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen and is reserved for hypoglycaemia where intravenous access has failed or hyperinsulinism is established, and in a hyperinsulinaemic infant it produces a brief rise followed by a rebound fall. It is a holding measure rather than the definitive answer when a drip can be sited. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Start empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin after cultures
options.rationale: Sepsis does cause neonatal hypoglycaemia and would demand exactly this, but it requires a risk factor or an unwell infant, and this baby is afebrile, well perfused and has a wholly sufficient alternative explanation in maternal diabetes. Treating an infection you have no evidence for leaves the glucose uncorrected. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Admit for intravenous 10 percent glucose with hourly glucose monitoring
options.rationale: A level that falls despite buccal gel and feeding has failed enteral management, and a blood glucose of 1.6 mmol/L carries a risk of neurological injury that does not depend on the baby looking symptomatic. Intravenous 10 percent glucose titrated against hourly levels is the definitive correction, and the admission also allows a true hypoglycaemia screen to be drawn if the requirement turns out to be high. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Infants of diabetic mothers are macrosomic and hyperinsulinaemic because maternal glucose crosses the placenta while maternal insulin does not, driving foetal islet hyperplasia that persists after the cord is cut. Screening with pre feed levels and treating with buccal glucose gel plus a feed is correct initial practice. The decision point in this question is that the repeat level has fallen rather than risen despite that treatment, which means enteral management has failed. A well appearing baby is not reassuring, because neonatal neuroglycopenia is frequently silent. Intravenous glucose with hourly monitoring is the answer, and persistent high glucose requirements should prompt a formal hypoglycaemia screen.
key_points: Foetal hyperinsulinism from maternal hyperglycaemia is the mechanism, and it resolves over the first days of life.
Buccal glucose gel with a feed is first line and is generally limited to two doses.
Absence of jitteriness, seizure or poor feeding does not make a low neonatal glucose safe.
A level that falls after treatment, rather than simply remaining low, signals failure of enteral management.
High intravenous glucose requirements suggest persistent hyperinsulinism and warrant a formal hypoglycaemia screen.
explanation.pearls: Escalate from buccal glucose gel to intravenous 10 percent glucose when the repeat pre feed level falls rather than rises, and draw the hypoglycaemia screen at the time of a low level rather than afterwards, because insulin, cortisol, growth hormone and ketones are only interpretable in the hypoglycaemic sample.

subtopic_detail: investigating an adolescent girl with heavy periods since menarche and lifelong easy bruising
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 14 year old girl referred with heavy periods. She reached menarche at twelve and says every period since then has been heavy, requiring a change of pad every hour on the first two days and causing her to miss school.

She has also had nosebleeds since early childhood, two of which needed nasal packing, and she bruises on her thighs without recalling any injury. She bled for several hours after a dental extraction at age ten. Her mother describes her own periods as heavy and had a postpartum haemorrhage after her second child. She takes no aspirin, no anti-inflammatory medication and no herbal preparations. On examination she has scattered bruises of differing ages over both thighs, no petechiae, no lymphadenopathy and no hepatosplenomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, bruises of varying age on both thighs, no petechiae or purpura, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no joint swelling or deformity
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (120-160), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100), platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (30-300), prothrombin time 12 seconds (11-14), activated partial thromboplastin time 41 seconds (25-38)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to assess megakaryocyte number and morphology
options.rationale: Marrow examination is directed at a production failure, which would show as cytopenias in one or more lineages with an abnormal film. Her platelet count is normal at 268 x10^9/L and her only cytopenia is a microcytic anaemia entirely explained by chronic menstrual iron loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Von Willebrand factor antigen and activity with a factor VIII level
options.rationale: A lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding pattern of menorrhagia, epistaxis, bruising and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction, with a normal platelet count, a normal prothrombin time and a mildly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time in a family with affected women, is von Willebrand disease until proven otherwise. The specific panel is needed because the screening tests are frequently normal in mild disease, and factor VIII is measured alongside because von Willebrand factor carries it and its reduction is what prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Factor IX assay with genetic testing for a haemophilia B carrier state
options.rationale: Haemophilia is X linked and produces deep bleeding into joints and muscles rather than a mucocutaneous pattern, and carrier females are usually only mildly affected. The absence of any joint bleeding and the strong female to female family pattern both point away from an X linked disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to identify a structural cause for her menstrual bleeding
options.rationale: Imaging looks for fibroids, polyps or adenomyosis, which are uncommon at fourteen and would not explain nosebleeds, bruising or bleeding after dental extraction. A structural diagnosis cannot account for bleeding at three separate anatomical sites since early childhood. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Antinuclear antibody with antiphospholipid antibodies and a lupus anticoagulant
options.rationale: A lupus anticoagulant does prolong the activated partial thromboplastin time and so is a reasonable thought when that test is abnormal, but it causes thrombosis rather than bleeding. Testing for it would explain the coagulation result while contradicting the entire clinical history. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

explanation.summary: Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, affecting around one percent of the population, and it is substantially underdiagnosed in adolescent girls whose heavy menstrual bleeding is accepted as normal. The pattern is mucocutaneous: menorrhagia, epistaxis, easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after dental or surgical procedures, in contrast to the deep joint and muscle bleeding of haemophilia. Autosomal inheritance means affected women appear across generations, which is why the maternal history matters. Screening tests are unreliable, since the platelet count is normal and the activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged only when factor VIII falls appreciably, so specific assays are required. Iron deficiency is almost universal and must be treated alongside, with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, tranexamic acid or desmopressin used to control the bleeding.
key_points: Mucocutaneous bleeding suggests a platelet or von Willebrand factor problem rather than a coagulation factor deficiency.
A normal platelet count and a normal or only mildly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time do not exclude the diagnosis.
Von Willebrand factor stabilises factor VIII, so factor VIII falls in more severe disease and prolongs the clotting time.
Autosomal inheritance means affected mothers and daughters are common, unlike X linked haemophilia.
Levels rise with stress, pregnancy and oestrogen, so repeat testing may be needed when suspicion is high.
explanation.pearls: Ask about nosebleeds and dental extractions in every adolescent with heavy periods, because a lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding history with a normal platelet count warrants specific von Willebrand assays rather than a pelvic ultrasound, and a single normal set of levels does not exclude the diagnosis since they rise with stress and oestrogen.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: advising a family about the single highest yield change when several sudden infant death risk factors are present together
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 week old boy for his immunisations. He was born at 35 weeks and is feeding well and gaining weight.

His mother mentions that she is exhausted. She tells you she smokes ten cigarettes a day outside the house, that the baby sleeps in a bassinet beside her bed on his back, and that when he wakes at three in the morning she feeds him lying down on the sofa in the lounge room and they both usually fall asleep there until the morning. She uses a light muslin wrap and the bassinet has a firm mattress and no bumpers or soft toys. She asks whether a home apnoea monitor would let her relax, because a friend has offered to lend one.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138/min, blood pressure not recorded, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and well grown, weight tracking along the 25th centile, chest clear, heart sounds normal with no murmur, anterior fontanelle soft

lead_in: Which single change would you advise first to reduce this baby's risk of sudden unexpected death?

options.text: Borrow the home apnoea monitor and use it whenever the baby sleeps
options.rationale: Domestic monitors detect central apnoea and bradycardia, and trials have never shown that they reduce sudden unexpected death, because the mechanism is not a detectable apnoea that a parent can interrupt. They also generate false alarms that worsen the exhaustion driving the unsafe sleeping in the first place. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Swaddle the baby more firmly with arms contained during every sleep
options.rationale: Firm wrapping with the hips able to flex and abduct is acceptable practice for a young infant sleeping on the back, but it is not the problem here and it becomes hazardous once a baby can roll. Adjusting the wrap addresses none of the three genuine risks in this history. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Feed the baby on a bed and return him to his own cot before sleeping
options.rationale: Sharing a sofa or armchair for sleep carries a far higher risk than any other sleep surface, because an infant wedges into the cushion gap or against the adult and cannot reposition, and this risk is multiplied by prematurity and maternal smoking, both present here. The practical advice is to move night feeds to a bed cleared of pillows and duvets so that falling asleep is survivable, and to return the baby to the bassinet in the parental room. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Move the bassinet out of the bedroom into a separate quiet nursery
options.rationale: This reverses the recommendation, since room sharing without bed sharing for the first six to twelve months is protective and separate room sleeping is associated with increased risk. The mother is already doing the right thing for the first part of the night. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Position the baby on his side with a rolled towel to stop him rolling
options.rationale: Side positioning was advised historically and has since been shown to be unstable, since infants roll from the side to the front, which is the highest risk position. Any device or prop used to maintain a position adds a suffocation hazard of its own. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

explanation.summary: Three risk factors stack in this history: prematurity at 35 weeks, maternal smoking, and unplanned sofa sleeping during night feeds. The mother has already got the supine position, the firm flat mattress and room sharing right, which is what makes the sofa the highest yield target. Sofa sharing carries a substantially greater risk than bed sharing, and it most often happens by accident when an exhausted parent feeds in a chair rather than as a planned arrangement. Advising a safer place to feed at night is therefore more useful than telling a tired mother simply not to fall asleep. Home apnoea monitors have no evidence of benefit and should not be offered as reassurance.
key_points: Supine positioning, a firm flat mattress, a clear cot and room sharing without bed sharing are the core protective measures.
Sofa and armchair sleeping carries the highest risk of any sleep surface for an infant.
Maternal smoking and prematurity are independent risk factors that multiply the risk of an unsafe sleep surface.
Home apnoea monitors have not been shown to reduce sudden unexpected death in infancy.
Side lying is not a safe alternative to supine because infants roll from the side onto the front.
explanation.pearls: Ask every exhausted parent where they actually feed at three in the morning rather than where the baby sleeps, because accidental sofa sleeping during night feeds is the commonest unrecognised high risk exposure and the fix is to move the feed to a cleared adult bed rather than to promise to stay awake.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sudden unexpected death in infancy
